A foundation for life
Welcome to Gillotts School
Gillotts is a high performing school where every student is valued as an individual, and is supported and encouraged to achieve their potential. We pride ourselves on being inclusive of all, developing young people who make a positive contribution to society now and in their future lives.
Gillotts school is located in Henley-on-Thames, Oxfordshire. It occupies a 33 acre site on the edge of the town, incorporating a large Victorian manor house and two of its associated cottages. There are extensive playing fields, as well as areas of grass, trees and woodland. There is no doubt that the beauty of the site contributes significantly to the atmosphere of the school.

Personal, Social and Health Education (PSHE)
Personal, Social and Health Education (PSHE)
These elements of the curriculum are combined into a subject termed ‘PSHE’ in both Key Stages 3 and 4. The citizenship and PSHE curriculum give students the knowledge, skills and understanding they need to lead confident, healthy and independent lives, and to become informed, active and responsible citizens, capable of forming good relationships and respecting the differences between people. We also aim to prepare students for the world of work, providing them with the knowledge, understanding, creativity and confidence to be wealth creators in their future lives. The core themes are Careers, Living in the Wider World, Health and wellbeing, Relationships, and Citizenship.
The delivery of PSHE is mapped across the curriculum, into tutor periods and also five discrete PSHE days which take place each year (two full days and three half days). A number of speakers come in to help deliver important content – including local police talking about county lines. We also use our links with The Henley College who deliver a session about post 16 options to Year 9 but also support us to deliver various topics including, this year, consent. Students also receive support from ta careers advisor. Students, parents, tutors, and the Learning Support team are informed of content prior to each day – to encourage wider discussion.
You can find more detail on the topics covered on each PSHE day in the document linked below.

Special educational needs and disability
A new national approach to special educational needs (SEN) provision has been in place since September 2014. The SEN Code of Practice covers the 0-25 age range and there is a clearer focus on the views of young people and on their role in decision making. There is also an emphasis on collaboration between education, health services and social care. The aim is to provide support that allows students with SEN to succeed in their education and to make a successful transition to adulthood. Oxfordshire County Council has developed a handbook entitled ‘Identifying and supporting Special Educational Needs in Oxfordshire schools and settings’ and we follow this guidance at Gillotts. Our practice is also described in our SEN Policy.
As our local authority, Oxfordshire County Council also publishes a local offer, setting out in one place information about the provision that is available for young people in our area. You can find more information here.

Careers information
Educating students for the future!
All students have access to an exciting programme of Careers Education, Information, Advice & Guidance that is tailored to inspire and promote all pathways to future education and employment. Working with local and national educational establishments and companies, some of whom are listed below, it will allow our students to make informed decisions about their post 16 options. A large majority of the careers education is delivered through the PSHE programme, but Mrs Allen is always looking to enhance the experience through bespoke opportunities.
Further details of the curriculum can be found at the bottom of this page. The next review will take place by August 2026.
You can support your children by accessing the Talking Futures campaign – a website of resources dedicated to help parents have meaningful career conversations with their children.
Our Careers Leader is Mrs Laura Allen. If you can offer experience in any capacity to broaden the careers education of students at Gillotts, please do contact Mrs Allen- 01491 574315 or lallen@@gillotts.org.
Students – If you would like an appointment to talk to our Careers Adviser, Charlotte van den Berghen, please see or email Mrs Allen, lallen@gillotts.org.
Parents – If you would like to support your child in their subject options for GCSE or post 16, please contact Mrs Allen who will be able to advise you and arrange an appointment with our Careers Adviser.
www.eclips-online.co.uk
eCLIPS is an easy-to-use online careers resource that provides regularly updated information on over 1,000 jobs and careers. For log-in details please see Ms Tristem.
oxmeinfo is a website packed full of the latest information for young people in Oxfordshire, helping them in all aspects of Education, Work and Life post 16.

pageCache.text:
House structure
Gillotts School has a House system, with three houses (Darwin, Orwell, and Pankhurst). Students are placed into one of the three houses upon admission to the school. Each House has a Head of House, an assistant Head of House, a team of tutors and a housebase with an administration team who are always available during the day for communication. This ensures that each student belongs to a small unit within the wider school community and receives as much personal support as possible.
During a daily tutorial period, all students in each tutor group are encouraged and helped to learn from each other in a supportive environment, thereby maximising their progress and achievement, as well as focussing on their well-being.
All houses have a bespoke tutor programme that they follow during their tutorial period. This programme helps to support students’ academic progress and personal development, delivering elements of our ‘Not by ourselves alone’ programme, careers, e-safety, and health and well-being, among others.
Where possible and appropriate, tutors and their tutor groups remain together as students progress through the school.
Information in the online student planner supports the tutor programme.
Our emotional health and wellbeing influence our cognitive development and learning as well as our physical and social health. Good mental health is important for helping people to develop and thrive. The World Health Organisation defines mental health as “a state of mental wellbeing that enables people to cope with the stresses of life, realise their abilities, learn well and work well, and contribute to their community”.
We support wellbeing of students and staff through:
These link to the NHS’s 5 steps to mental wellbeing.
Gillotts’ motto is ‘Non Nobis Solum’ which translates as ‘Not by Ourselves Alone’. We link this to our three key values of kindness, respect and not doing harm. These support the school to be a community to which all students can feel connected and, in time, develop a sense of belonging.
Our Senior Mental Health Lead is Matt Druce, Assistant Headteacher. Our Adult Mental Health First Aider is Charlotte Alder, Subject Leader Performing Arts.

pageCache.text:
Not by ourselves alone
‘Not by ourselves alone’ is a translation of ‘Non Nobis Solum’, and is a pastoral programme that focuses on three key values that we hold important through our school Mission Statement:
Gillotts is a high performing school where every student is valued as an individual, and is supported and encouraged to achieve their potential. We pride ourselves on being inclusive of all, developing young people who make a positive contribution to society now and in their future lives
The values of Respect, Kindness, and Living without harm are taught, encouraged and developed through our tutor programme, assemblies, and through extra curricular opportunities, projects and ideas led by students and tutors. The programme has been introduced through our membership with PiXL, a partnership of roughly half of secondary schools nationwide, where best practice, ideas and resources are shared to develop school outcomes. PiXL introduced a scheme called ‘Them and Us’, focusing on the three values above, providing resources for us to adapt to our needs.
The programme has been extremely successful so far in enhancing the sense of community that is so important within school. Acts of kindness are rewarded through our achievement point system, and our school twitter account @gillottshenley keeps our wider local community up to date with all the fantastic projects, schemes, fundraising and other events going on!

pageCache.text:
Help for families
We understand that it’s hard to be a parent and at times children and families need some extra support. We want you to know that it is OK to ask for help.
Why might you need help?
Overuse of internet, behaviour, anxiety, school refusal, friendship concerns, parenting support classes, medical advice, housing, safeguarding, domestic abuse, finding out about and accessing external services, SEND, drugs, alcohol, gangs, online safety…
Have a conversation with a member of school staff that you know and trust. You can discuss what’s going well and any difficulties you and your family may be experiencing and they will be able to help you to get the right support. Sometimes, just having a conversation can really help.
As well as from the school itself, you could also get help from your wider family and support networks, or from professionals in the community that you know like health visitors, midwives, doctors, or the voluntary sector. You can get help for domestic abuse this this website.
They may suggest that you share the things you discuss with other agencies who could be in a better position to help and that will involve completing what’s known as a Strengths and Needs form. They will ensure that any personal information you give is only shared with your permission.
Here is Oxfordshire’s Early Help Guide for Families
The documents linked below also offer advice and guidance for parents on a range of topics including supporting learning and revision at home, emotional wellbeing, online bullying and more.

Wider pastoral structure
The wider pastoral structure ensures that a range of help is available for students’ individual needs. The pastoral team, including tutors, assistant heads of house, heads of house, house administrators, student support administrators and wider support staff, work collaboratively to ensure that early concerns are noted, identified and supported through the interventions available on the school site.
These include, but are not restricted to:
Counselling School Health Nurse ELSA (Emotional Literacy Support) Emotional well being support Guitar Yoga Mindfulness Mentoring – provided by NOMAD – a local Youth & Community project that supports children, young people and families Young Carers support Anime club LGBT support
Students aged 16 and above, or who are Gillick competent, are able to access counselling at school or support from the school nurse confidentially, and parental consent will not be required, though students will be encouraged to involve their parents.

On this page you will find additional information about the Learning Support Team – the intervention and support offered and some activities to complete to get you ready to join us in September.
We hope you will find these resources useful and it will help your child to feel less anxious about joining Gillotts School in September. We can’t wait to find out all about them from the activities they complete.
If you have any questions, please do not hesitate to contact the SENDCo, Miss Claire Collyer on ccollyer@gillotts.org
Looking forward to seeing you all in September!

Years 10-11
Years 10 and 11 Curriculum
We believe that our curriculum is flexible enough to meet the individual needs of all our students in Years 10 and 11. Some subjects (the core) are compulsory, but we also offer the opportunity for students to make choices about subjects to study, supporting their core curriculum. We cover all the entitlement areas required by the National Curriculum.
The core subjects which all students study include English, mathematics, science, physical education, religious studies and PSHE. The amount of time devoted to each subject is as follows:
Timetable allocation
7 hours per fortnight
7 hours per fortnight
8 hours per fortnight
4 hours per fortnight
2 hours per fortnight
While ICT is no longer taught as a discrete subject, it is used as a tool to support learning across the whole curriculum.
In addition, students are able to choose from a wide range of option choices. These include both traditional GCSEs as well as a range of other courses which are equivalent to GCSEs. Students have four slots on their timetable which are filled with option subjects (5 hours per slot).

Years 7-9
Year 7-9 Curriculum The curriculum followed by students in Years 7-9 is based on the National Curriculum Key Stage 3 programmes of study. Students follow a common curriculum comprising:
Timetable allocation
2 hours per fortnight
Carousel (Computer Science, Design Technology, Drama & Food)
4 hours per fortnight
8 hours per fortnight (Y7) 7 hours per fortnight (Y8-9)
3 hours per fortnight
3 hours per fortnight
7 hours per fortnight
Modern Foreign Languages
6 hours per fortnight
3 hours per fortnight
Physical Education & Dance
4 hours per fortnight
2 hours per fortnight (Y7) 3 hours per fortnight (Y8-9)
6 hours per fortnight
In MFL, all students are taught French throughout Years 7-9. At the start of Year 7 all students are taught French in mixed ability teaching groups. However, during Year 7, the classes are re-set according to ability with the top two classes in each band (4 in total) picking up a second language (either German or Spanish). In this case three hours per fortnight are spent on French and three hours on the second language. The MFL Subject Leader is responsible for deciding which second language students will study.
There is a carousel of four subjects (computer science, design technology, drama and food). These subjects are taught in pairs with students following two of the subjects for half the year (computer science & design technology or food & drama) and the other two in the second half. The specific details of what is taught in each subject in Years 7-9 and how student progress is assessed are contained within the Years 7-9 Curriculum Guides.
Setting arrangements
We use a variety of ways to set students in different subjects and in different years depending on what is the most appropriate context for individual students’ learning. In all classes (both mixed ability ones and those set by ability) there is a range of ability. To take account of these differences all staff have a responsibility when planning work to meet the needs of all students. This will involve, at different times, adapting tasks; providing different resources; developing extension work; providing a variety of learning styles and environments; setting individual goals; giving different levels of support, and offering a variety of ways to demonstrate knowledge and understanding.
